fullText:
Summary: Singer (Sri Lanka) PLC (SINS.N0000) is having a boom: sales rose 46% and profit 83% in the year to March 2026, and the first quarter of this year was up another 44%. But at Rs 74.10 the share trades at 4.0x its NAV of Rs 18.41 and 10.8x trailing earnings, which assumes today's very high return on equity (about 40%) lasts. Singer's profits are cyclical (it made a loss in 2023/24 and almost nothing in 2022/23) and the group carries a lot of debt to fund customer credit. Allowing ROE to fade towards its long-run average, the methods put fair value at about Rs 45, so the price is about 65% above it. I'd buy at up to about Rs 38 and treat under Rs 34 as a strong buy.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 74.10 (CSE closing price, 2026-11-06). Please check it live. In April–June 2026 it traded between Rs 66.00 and Rs 92.50; it closed the year to March 2026 at Rs 77.00, up from Rs 33.80 a year earlier.
Three months to 30 June 2026 (group, unaudited): revenue rose 41% to Rs 38.7bn and profit attributable rose 44% to Rs 2.15bn. EPS was Rs 1.84 against Rs 1.28.
What drove it: strong demand for consumer durables (gross profit up 42%), with selling and administrative costs up a slower 32%, so operating profit rose 59%. Net finance costs more than doubled to Rs 972mn as borrowing grew.
Year to March 2026 (group): revenue Rs 128.6bn (up 46%), profit after tax Rs 7.66bn (up 83%), EPS Rs 6.29 (Rs 3.43), return on average net assets 40%, NAV Rs 17.07, dividends Rs 1.84 (29% of profit).
Debt: total debt Rs 82.3bn and net debt Rs 74.7bn at March 2026, 3.4x equity (up from 2.6x). Much of this funds customer credit and the finance subsidiary (Singer Finance), whose public deposits doubled to Rs 13.7bn.
Cycle: EPS was Rs 3.51 (2021/22), Rs 0.01 (2022/23), a loss of Rs 0.14 (2023/24), Rs 3.43 (2024/25) and Rs 6.29 (2025/26).

Methods
NAV (Rs 18.41): 4.0x, so it fails your NAV rule by a wide margin.
Return on equity: about 40% in the year to March 2026 (29% the year before); it was -1% in 2023/24 and 1% in 2022/23.
P/E: 10.8x trailing EPS of Rs 6.85. Year-end P/E: 12.2x (2026), 9.7x (2025).
Dividends: Rs 1.84 for 2025/26 (paid in four interim dividends), a 2.5% yield; Rs 0.50 was paid in the first quarter of this year.
Debt: net debt 3.4x equity, interest cover 4.2x.
Justified price to book: Rs 15.0 / 25.5 / 40.3 across the cases, weighted Rs 25.3.
P/E method: Rs 38.5 / 68.4 / 93.5, weighted Rs 64.5.
Residual income: Rs 20.6 / 42.8 / 88.2, weighted Rs 45.2.
Dividend model: Rs 10.7 / 19.8 / 31.3 (not used in the fair value).

Singer pays out under a third of its profit, so a dividend model understates it; its free cash flow is swamped by customer-credit growth, so a cash-flow DCF isn't reliable. The P/E method is the most generous because it applies a normal multiple to boom-time earnings. Price to book is the strictest because it assumes ROE settles at 24% straight away.

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity: 21% / 19% / 17.5% (higher than for other companies because of the cycle and the debt).
Long-run ROE (price to book): 18% / 24% / 30%.
ROE path (residual income): 30% falling to 18% / 38% falling to 22% / 42% falling to 28%.
Long-term growth: 5% / 6% / 7%.
EPS for the year to March 2027 × P/E: 5.5 × 7 / 7.6 × 9 / 8.5 × 11.
Average of the three methods: Rs 24.7 / Rs 45.6 / Rs 74.0.
Common: Sri Lankan 7–10-year government bonds yield about 12% (October 2026). In the base case, the rest of the year grows about 15% on last year's, giving EPS of about Rs 7.60 for the year to March 2027. Over the last ten years ROE averaged under 20%.

Fair value and buy price
Fair value: weighting 30/50/20 gives about Rs 45 (2.4x NAV), so Rs 74.10 is about 65% above it.
Buy price: a 15% margin of safety gives Rs 38.30, and 25% gives Rs 33.80.
Plan for 500 shares: 200 at up to Rs 45.00, 150 at up to Rs 38.30 and 150 at up to Rs 33.80. That averages about Rs 39.63, about Rs 19,815, against Rs 37,050 at Rs 74.10.
Realism: Rs 45 needs about a 39% fall. The share was Rs 33.80 in March 2025, so it has been there recently, and cyclical shares can fall that far quickly when demand or interest rates turn, but it isn't likely while profits are still rising.

Sensitivity (residual income base case, Rs per share)
Cost of equity 17%: 40.8 / 55.0 / 81.7 for long-run ROE of 18% / 22% / 28%.
Cost of equity 19%: 32.4 / 42.8 / 62.3.
Cost of equity 21%: 26.5 / 34.4 / 49.1.
Today's price needs ROE to stay near 30% or more for many years.

What would change my view
Supports a higher value: ROE staying above 30% through the next downturn; debt falling relative to equity; a higher dividend payout; lower interest rates, which cut funding costs and support demand for credit-financed purchases.
Supports a lower value: a consumer slowdown or tighter import or credit rules; rising interest rates squeezing margins on hire-purchase sales; bad debts rising after rapid credit growth; net debt climbing above 3.4x equity; earnings falling back as in 2022–2024.

These are my estimates from the annual reports for the years to March 2025 and March 2026 and the interim reports to June 2026. The interim figures are unaudited, so check the price before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
